introduction-the-ultimate-game-of-tetris.core: The scheduler places each Pending Pod on a node in two phases: filtering (which nodes can fit it, given resources, taints, affinity, volumes and ports) and scoring (which feasible node is best, considering balance, spreading and affinities), then binds the Pod. It uses requests, not actual usage.

first_principles.problem: Pods stay Pending while nodes look underutilised in monitoring dashboards.

analogy.title: Tetris with rules
analogy.story: Each piece must fit the space and obey colour rules, and you choose the spot that keeps the board tidy.
analogy.breaks: Tetris pieces have fixed shapes; Pod requests are declared and may not match real usage.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Lower inflated CPU request or add capacity.

code.text:
kubectl describe pod api-7f9 | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
# 0/12 nodes are available: 8 Insufficient cpu, 4 node(s) had untolerated taint {gpu: true}

check.q: Does the scheduler use actual CPU usage when placing Pods?
check.a: No; it uses the Pods' resource requests.

requests-vs-limits-the-foundation-of-all.core: Requests are what the scheduler reserves and guarantees; limits are the maximum a container may use. CPU over the limit is throttled (CFS quota); memory over the limit causes an OOM kill. Requests also set CPU shares under contention and determine QoS class and eviction order.

first_principles.problem: Pods without memory limits trigger node OOMs; pods with tight CPU limits are throttled despite idle CPUs.
derivation: Set **memory limits** to prevent runaway use.

analogy.title: A restaurant reservation and a table size limit
analogy.story: The reservation guarantees seats; the limit stops a party from taking over the whole room.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants ask politely; the kernel kills memory overusers instantly.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Guaranteed memory, burstable CPU, no OOM surprises.

check.q: What happens when a container exceeds its memory limit?

bin-packing-filling-the-boxes-efficientl.core: Bin packing places Pods to use node capacity efficiently. The default scorer spreads load (LeastAllocated); MostAllocated or RequestedToCapacityRatio pack tightly so autoscalers can remove empty nodes. Multi-dimensional resources (CPU, memory, GPU) create fragmentation, where nodes have leftover capacity of the wrong shape.

first_principles.problem: Nodes average 40% CPU but 95% memory, so new Pods can't fit and costs climb.

analogy.title: Packing a removal van
analogy.story: Heavy boxes fill weight capacity while bulky light boxes fill space; mix them well or the van is 'full' half-empty.
analogy.breaks: Vans are packed once; Pods come and go continuously.

check.q: What is resource fragmentation in scheduling?
check.a: Nodes have free capacity in some dimensions but not others, so new Pods can't fit despite unused resources.

the-fairness-problem-dominant-resource-f.core: When many tenants share a cluster with multiple resource types, fairness isn't obvious. Dominant Resource Fairness allocates so each tenant's dominant share (the largest fraction of any single resource they use) is equalised. It's strategy-proof and used in Mesos, YARN and batch schedulers like Kueue and Volcano.

first_principles.problem: A CPU-heavy team and a memory-heavy team argue about who gets more of a shared cluster.
truths: Fairness on one resource ignores others.

analogy.title: Sharing a buffet fairly between a vegetarian and a meat lover
analogy.story: Equalise how much of each person's favourite dish they get, not just the number of plates.
analogy.breaks: Buffets refill; cluster resources are finite at any moment.

example.title: DRF calculation
flow: DRF gives A 3 tasks per B's 2 to equalise dominant shares

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Both teams get equal shares of what they need most.

check.q: What is a tenant's dominant share in DRF?
check.a: The maximum, across resource types, of the fraction of the cluster's resource that tenant uses.

quality-of-service-qos-classes.core: Kubernetes assigns each Pod a QoS class from its requests and limits. When a node runs short of memory, the kubelet evicts BestEffort Pods first, then Burstable Pods using the most above their requests, and Guaranteed Pods last. The kernel's OOM score adjustment follows the same ordering.

first_principles.problem: A critical payment Pod is evicted under memory pressure while low-priority batch Pods survive.
truths: Something must be evicted under pressure.

analogy.title: Airline seat classes during overbooking
analogy.story: Standby passengers are bumped first, economy next and first class last.
analogy.breaks: Airlines compensate bumped passengers; evicted Pods simply restart elsewhere if possible.

code.text:
kubectl get pod payments-0 -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
# Guaranteed

check.q: Which QoS class is evicted first under node memory pressure?

defining-the-three-qos-classes.core: Guaranteed: every container has CPU and memory requests equal to limits. Burstable: at least one container has a request or limit but doesn't meet Guaranteed. BestEffort: no container has any requests or limits. CPU manager static policy can pin exclusive cores for Guaranteed Pods with integer CPU requests.

first_principles.problem: A team sets requests equal to limits for memory only and is surprised the Pod is Burstable.
truths: Guaranteed requires CPU and memory, all containers.
Any request or limit means at least Burstable.
Exclusive CPUs need integer Guaranteed requests.
derivation: **Guaranteed**: requests = limits for CPU & memory in all containers.
Use **static CPU manager** for latency-critical Guaranteed Pods.

analogy.title: Hotel bookings
analogy.story: A fixed room booked and paid (Guaranteed), a room with possible upgrade (Burstable), or a walk-in hoping for space (BestEffort).
analogy.breaks: Hotels can move you; Kubernetes assigns QoS automatically from the spec.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Guaranteed QoS; eligible for exclusive cores.

check.a: Every container has CPU and memory requests equal to their limits.

priorityclasses-and-preemption.core: PriorityClasses assign integer priorities to Pods. When a high-priority Pod can't be scheduled, the scheduler may preempt (evict) lower-priority Pods to make room, respecting PDBs on a best-effort basis. preemptionPolicy: Never lets Pods queue ahead without evicting others. System classes protect critical cluster components.

first_principles.problem: During a capacity crunch, production Pods stay Pending while batch jobs hold the resources.
truths: Not all workloads are equally important.
Evicting lower-value work can be acceptable.

analogy.title: An ambulance on a busy road
analogy.story: Other cars pull over so it can pass.
analogy.breaks: Cars resume their journey; preempted Pods must reschedule and may lose work.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Prod Pods evict batch when capacity is short.

code.text:
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: {name: prod-high}
value: 100000
---
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: {name: batch-low}
value: 1000
preemptionPolicy: Never

check.a: The Pod gets queue priority but won't evict other Pods to be scheduled.
